title: Package Layout

writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
src/main.rs defines the default binary and src/lib.rs defines the library target. Additional binaries and integration tests have conventional directories that keep tooling automatic.

Cargo recognizes conventional paths, which lets a small project grow without custom build configuration. `src/main.rs` is the default binary entry point. `src/lib.rs` defines a library target that other crates and integration tests can import. Additional binaries can live under `src/bin/`, while external tests live under `tests/`. These paths describe targets, not just folders for tidiness.

In the sample, `demo::answer()` calls the library from the binary. The name before the double colon is the library crate name, normally derived from the package name unless configured otherwise. A binary in the same package still uses the library through its public interface. This is useful discipline: the CLI can remain a thin layer around reusable logic, and integration tests can exercise the same API that a user imports.

Try moving a function from `main.rs` into `lib.rs`, marking it public, and calling it from both the binary and a test in `tests/`. Confirm which imports compile and which private helpers remain inaccessible. Keep module files inside the appropriate target; creating a file by itself does not make Rust compile it unless it is a recognized target or declared from the module tree. A conventional layout reduces configuration surprises, but choose a new crate only when the code deserves its own package boundary.
